```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

```{r}
library(pgmcompR)
```

A causal Bayesian network reads its arcs as direct causal effects. Under
that reading, the intervention $do(X = x)$ replaces the CPD of $X$ by a
point mass and leaves every other mechanism intact (the truncated
factorization). Conditioning and intervening then differ whenever $X$ and
the outcome share a common cause.

## Observing versus doing

Kidney stone size $Z$ influences both the choice of treatment $X$ and
recovery $Y$:

```{r}
st <- list(Size = c("small", "large"), Treatment = c("A", "B"), Recovery = c("no", "yes"))
kidney <- bayesian_network(list(c("Size", "Treatment"), c("Size", "Recovery"), c("Treatment", "Recovery")), states = st)
kidney <- add_cpd(kidney, cpd("Size", c(small = 0.51, large = 0.49)))
kidney <- add_cpd(kidney, cpd("Treatment", c(0.25, 0.75, 0.77, 0.23), "Size", st))
kidney <- add_cpd(kidney, cpd("Recovery", c(0.07, 0.93, 0.13, 0.87, 0.27, 0.73, 0.31, 0.69),
                              c("Treatment", "Size"), st))
query(kidney, "Recovery", list(Treatment = "A"))
query(kidney, "Recovery", list(Treatment = "B"))
do_query(kidney, "Recovery", list(Treatment = "A"))
do_query(kidney, "Recovery", list(Treatment = "B"))
```

Observationally, treatment B looks better (Simpson's paradox). Under
intervention, treatment A is better in every stratum and overall.
`intervene()` returns the mutilated network itself:

```{r}
parents(intervene(kidney, list(Treatment = "A")), "Treatment")
```

## Adjustment

When only observational data are available, the back door criterion says
which covariates to adjust for. A set $Z$ satisfies it relative to $(X, Y)$
if no element of $Z$ descends from $X$ and $Z$ blocks every path from $X$ to
$Y$ that starts with an arrow into $X$.

```{r}
is_backdoor_set(kidney, "Treatment", "Recovery", "Size")
adjustment_sets(kidney, "Treatment", "Recovery")
identify_effect(kidney, "Treatment", "Recovery")
```

The adjustment formula from observational quantities reproduces the
interventional answer:

```{r}
pz <- factor_values(query(kidney, "Size"))
py <- sapply(st$Size, function(z) factor_values(query(kidney, "Recovery", list(Treatment = "A", Size = z)))[2])
sum(pz * py)
```

### M-bias

Adjusting for more is not always better. In the M structure, $M$ is a
collider; conditioning on it opens a path between $X$ and $Y$:

```{r}
m <- dag(list(c("A", "X"), c("A", "M"), c("B", "M"), c("B", "Y"), c("X", "Y")))
is_backdoor_set(m, "X", "Y", character())
is_backdoor_set(m, "X", "Y", "M")
```

## Latent confounding and the front door

When the confounder is unobserved, the back door is closed to us, but a
mediator that intercepts every causal path can still identify the effect:

```{r}
fd <- dag(list(c("U", "Smoking"), c("U", "Cancer"), c("Smoking", "Tar"), c("Tar", "Cancer")))
identify_effect(fd, "Smoking", "Cancer", latent = "U")
```

Without such a mediator, the effect is not identifiable from these graphs
by the back door or front door criteria, and pgmcompR says so instead of
returning a number:

```{r, error = TRUE}
bow <- dag(list(c("U", "X"), c("U", "Y"), c("X", "Y")))
identify_effect(bow, "X", "Y", latent = "U")
```

A complete identification algorithm (Shpitser and Pearl's ID) is planned
for a later version.

## Counterfactuals in structural causal models

A structural causal model (SCM) makes every endogenous variable a
deterministic function of its parents and of exogenous noise. Counterfactual
queries follow three steps: abduction (update the noise given the evidence),
action (apply the intervention) and prediction.

```{r}
model <- scm(
  exogenous = list(U_x = c(low = 0.6, high = 0.4), U_y = c(robust = 0.7, frail = 0.3)),
  parents = list(Treated = "U_x", Died = c("Treated", "U_y")),
  states = list(Treated = c("no", "yes"), Died = c("no", "yes")),
  equations = list(
    Treated = function(U_x) if (U_x == "high") "yes" else "no",
    Died = function(Treated, U_y) if (U_y == "frail" && Treated == "no") "yes" else "no"
  )
)
model
```

A treated patient survived. Would they have died without treatment?

```{r}
counterfactual(model, "Died", evidence = list(Treated = "yes", Died = "no"),
               interventions = list(Treated = "no"))
```

Survival under treatment says nothing about frailty here, so the
counterfactual probability of death equals the prior frailty, 0.3. This is
not the same as $P(\text{Died} \mid do(\text{Treated} = \text{no}))$ for a
fresh patient only because, in this simple model, the evidence happens to be
uninformative about $U_y$.
